items.title: Building a Career in Web Development with AI-Powered Full Stack Skills
items.abstract: Web development is changing as businesses adopt new technologies to improve their digital services. Companies need websites, web applications, and software platforms that offer a smooth user experience, protect customer data, and support business growth. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is adding new capabilities to this process by helping developers write code, test applications, solve technical problems, and build intelligent features. Full-stack development gives professionals the skills to work on both the front end and the back end of an application. When combined with AI-powered development tools, these skills can help developers build useful digital products and adapt to changing industry requirements. For aspiring professionals, a career in web development involves more than learning a programming language. It requires an understanding of application design, databases, APIs, testing, deployment, and security. AI knowledge can extend these skills by helping developers automate routine tasks and integrate intelligent services into web applications. The Changing Role of Web Developers Web developers traditionally build and maintain websites and applications by writing code, connecting databases, testing features, and fixing errors. Modern development also requires collaboration with designers, product managers, security teams, and other engineers. AI tools are changing parts of this workflow. Developers can use them to generate code suggestions, explain unfamiliar functions, draft documentation, and create initial test cases. This may reduce time spent on some repetitive tasks. However, AI-generated code is not always correct or secure. Developers must understand the underlying logic and check the output before using it in a live application. They must also confirm that the code meets performance requirements and follows the project's standards. This change increases the value of problem-solving and technical judgement. Developers who understand programming fundamentals can evaluate AI suggestions more effectively than those who depend on generated code without understanding it. A career in web development can therefore benefit from a balanced skill set that combines coding knowledge, AI literacy, communication, and continuous learning. Research and Market Trends Shaping Career Opportunities Industry research provides useful evidence about the skills and technology roles expected to become more important. These trends support the case for learning full-stack development and AI, although they do not guarantee employment for individual candidates.Learners exploring a Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can use this growing intersection of software engineering and artificial intelligence as a starting point for developing industry-relevant skills. Global employment outlook The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies software and application developers among the fastest-growing job categories through 2030. It also lists AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy among the skills expected to increase in importance. The report draws on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 55 economies. Its findings indicate that technology-related changes will affect both job requirements and workforce training. For aspiring web developers, this highlights the importance of learning core programming skills while remaining open to new tools and development methods. India's technology industry NASSCOM's Annual Strategic Review 2025 estimated that India's technology industry generated more than US$282.6 billion in revenue in FY2025, including hardware. It also projected that the industry could reach US$300 billion in FY2026. Engineering research and development, digital engineering, and global capability centres are among the areas contributing to India's technology ecosystem. These organisations support software development, product engineering, cloud services, and business transformation. This industry context creates a reason for learners to develop relevant technical skills. However, overall industry revenue is not the same as the number of available web development jobs. Actual hiring depends on employer requirements, business conditions, experience, and technical ability. Research on AI-assisted programming A controlled experiment published by researchers associated with Microsoft Research examined the effect of GitHub Copilot on a JavaScript programming task. Participants with access to the AI assistant completed the specified task 55.8% faster than participants in the control group. This result demonstrates the potential value of AI assistance in a defined setting. It does not mean that every software project will be completed at the same speed. Complex applications still require design, testing, security reviews, debugging, and coordination between team members. The practical lesson is to use AI tools to support development while retaining human responsibility for the final product. Core Skills for a Career in Full Stack Development A strong technical foundation helps developers build applications that work reliably. AI tools can support this process, but they cannot replace an understanding of how software systems operate. Front-end development Front-end development focuses on the interface users interact with. HTML provides structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds interactive features. Developers can also learn frameworks such as React to create reusable components and manage complex interfaces. Responsive design and accessibility are important because applications must work across different devices and meet the needs of different users. AI assistants can help create initial interface components, but developers must check the design, usability, browser compatibility, and performance. Back-end development Back-end development handles application logic, data processing, authentication, and communication between services. Common technologies include Node.js, Python, Java, and their related frameworks. Developers should understand how to create APIs, manage user permissions, validate inputs, and handle errors. These skills help them build applications that are reliable and secure. Databases and APIs Databases store information such as customer profiles, orders, transactions, and product records. Knowledge of SQL, database design, data validation, and access control helps developers manage this information. APIs connect different systems. A web application may use them to communicate with payment gateways, cloud platforms, analytics services, or AI models. Understanding these connections is essential when building complete applications. Cloud, DevOps, and security Web development does not end when the code is written. Applications must be deployed, monitored, updated, and protected against security threats. Developers can benefit from learning Git, automated testing, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), containers, and cloud platforms. They should also understand secure authentication, data privacy, and the risks of exposing confidential information to unapproved AI tools. Using AI Tools to Build Better Applications AI can support developers throughout the application lifecycle, from planning to maintenance. Its usefulness depends on the task, the quality of the input, and the developer's ability to evaluate the output. Code generation and debugging AI coding assistants can suggest functions, explain error messages, and create initial versions of repetitive code. Developers can use these suggestions to explore possible solutions and learn unfamiliar technologies. Before accepting generated code, they should review the logic, run tests, and check for security issues. This practice helps reduce the risk of introducing errors into an application. AI-powered application features Generative AI can help businesses add features such as chat assistants, document summaries, natural-language search, and personalised recommendations. For example, a customer support application could use an AI model to answer questions based on approved company documents. The full stack developer would build the user interface, manage access controls, connect APIs, and create the systems required to retrieve relevant information. Retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects AI models with information retrieved from selected data sources. It can help applications produce responses based on relevant documents rather than relying only on information learned during model training. AI agents can use approved tools to complete defined multi-step tasks. These systems require clear permissions, monitoring, error handling, and human oversight when actions carry risk. Learning these concepts can help developers move beyond basic websites and explore more advanced applications. items.title: Building Resilient Telecom Operators through Artificial Intelligence: A CTE-Based Approach to Autonomous Network and Business Operations
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing where competitive advantage comes from in telecommunications. It used to depend mainly on network assets - spectrum, infrastructure, reach. Increasingly, it depends on how intelligent, adaptable, and resilient the systems running those assets are. This paper builds on the Comprehensive Techno-Economic (CTE) Model and its AI-augmented extension (AI-CTE) to propose a resilience framework that covers both autonomous network operations and autonomous business operations. Previous AI-CTE work formalized AI maturity, augmentation, dependency, and governance constructs, but mostly at the Technical Level. This paper extends that work in two directions. First, it introduces a Network Resilience Composite, combining the existing AI Resilience Score with a new Shock Absorption Capacity metric to quantify how well autonomous networks withstand and recover from disruptive events. Second, it develops three new AI-augmented equations at the Business Level - product and service resilience, customer and revenue resilience, and workforce resilience - which together make up a Business Resilience Index. These technical and business constructs, together with an Environmental/Governance Resilience Index, are combined into a single Telecom Operator Resilience Index (TORI). An illustrative application, extending a previously published case study, shows how the index can expose a gap between strong technical autonomy and weaker business-level resilience, giving operators concrete guidance on where to prioritize AI investment. The paper closes with an implementation roadmap and a discussion of limitations and future research directions. items.title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. Each dialogue has a control version without the requests, so that only systems that have stored the target can earn credit for forgetting. Across the paired versions, five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. Across all evaluated systems and backbones, no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none at all. These systems either leave the requested information extractable under simple attacks or delete far more than requested. Memory unlearning therefore remains an open challenge for agent memory design. We release our data and code at https://github.com/Nboxff/bemula-benchmark.

items.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

items.title: Can I handover? A systematic literature review on handover in emergency department interactions
items.abstract: Effective communication during handover in Emergency Department (ED) is extremely important. Despite the abundance of studies on handover interactions in EDs, the task of conducting a systematic review on this specific research topic has proven to be challenging. This is due to the lack of inclusion of review procedures, making it difficult for scholars to replicate or interpret the findings. This study aims to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) concerning interactions during handover in ED. The review processes consisted of five essential methodological steps, guided by a review protocol and involved formulating research questions, implementing systematic searching strategies to identify relevant studies from established databases such as Scopus, Web of Science, Science Direct, Emerald, Taylor Francis, Springer Link, and Sage Journals, quality appraisal, data extraction, and analysis. 2985 articles were identified, 249 articles left after screening, and 17 articles were reviewed. The key of the study is to answer the question; ‘How do health personnel communicate during handoffs in the EDs? Themes were also discovered based on the thematic analysis: (1) handoff tool, (most widely used are: are SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation), iSoBAR (Identify, Situation, Observation, Background, Agreed plan, Read back), I-PASS (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by receiver), and IDEAS (Identification, Diagnosis, Status, Actions, warning Signs and Symptoms); (2) Closed loop communication (CLC); (3) Self embodied knowledge; (4) verbal or written and two influencing themes: (5) environment and (6) people. These six themes were furthermore divided into nine sub-themes.

items.title: Can Zero-Shot Large Language Models Be Trusted for Credit-Risk Prediction? An Explainability Audit Against LightGBM on Loan Default Data
items.abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) offer a low-barrier route to credit-risk prediction, but regulated use requires evidence on discrimination, probability reliability, and auditable decision patterns. We compare four open-source LLMs (Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B) with LightGBM on 396,030 U.S. LendingClub loans issued from 2007 to 2016. Treating loans as independent and identically distributed observations from this pooled cross-sectional population, we evaluate every model on the same random 20% holdout. All models receive the same 21 structured predictors and output repayment probabilities. We audit empirical decision patterns with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP); separately, each LLM supplies one context-free positive, negative, or neutral direction per feature, which we treat as its feature-level self-explanation. LightGBM achieved ROC-AUC 0.724, PR-AUC 0.907, and Brier score 0.141, compared with 0.669, 0.880, and 0.204 for the best-discriminating LLM, Gemma-2-9B. An equal-weight LightGBM–Gemma ensemble did not improve any metric. In an eight-cycle SHAP audit, each LLM shared six or seven of LightGBM’s ten most important features; these self-explanations agreed with empirical SHAP directions for only 33–67% of assessable top features, revealing self-explanation unfaithfulness under this directional criterion. A nested four-cycle estimate reproduced every LLM’s top-10 set and nearly identical importance ranks, although small magnitude and distribution shifts were statistically detectable. These results caution against standalone zero-shot LLM use in credit risk and support calibration checks, explainability audits, interpretable benchmarks, and human oversight before deployment.

items.title: Causal AI and Structural Causal Models in Foundation Systems: Counterfactual Reasoning, Invariant Representation Learning, and Out-of-Distribution Robustness
items.abstract: Abstract—Contemporary foundation models—encompassing large language models (LLMs) and vision-language transformers—achieve state-of-the-art predictive performance by identifying complex statistical correlations across massive training distributions. However, standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) operates fundamentally at the lowest rung of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy: the observational level (associational correlation). Consequently, state-of-the-art deep networks suffer from critical failure modes in safety-critical deployments: spurious correlations, algorithmic bias, catastrophic out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization failure under covariate shift, and an intrinsic inability to compute counterfactual queries ('what would have occurred had treatment X been altered?'). Causal Artificial Intelligence (Causal AI) provides the mathematical foundations to bridge associative deep learning with interventional and counterfactual reasoning through Structural Causal Models (SCMs), do-calculus, and invariant representation learning. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Causal AI integrated into modern foundation models. We formalize Pearl's structural causal framework, establish the mathematical bounds of Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP) and Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM), and derive differentiable score-based directed acyclic graph (DAG) discovery using continuous algebraic constraints (NOTEARS). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise benchmarking testbed across three high-stakes domain corpora: clinical biomedical counterfactual trial synthesis, algorithmic credit fairness under confounders, and visual out-of-distribution robustness under adversarial domain perturbations. Our empirical results demonstrate that incorporating structural causal regularization into transformer representations improves OOD generalization accuracy by 34.6% over standard empirical risk minimization while reducing spurious attribute reliance by 72.8%. Concurrently, interventional do-calculus routing suppresses counterfactual hallucinations in clinical decision support from 28.4% down to 4.2%. Finally, we formulate open research directions in causal representation learning from high-dimensional pixels, automated unobserved confounder discovery, and causal safety alignment for autonomous foundation agents. Index Terms—Causal AI, Structural Causal Models (SCMs), Counterfactual Reasoning, Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM), Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, Do-Calculus, Causal Discovery, Out-of-Distribution Robustness.

items.title: CCD-MAF: A Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram-driven Multi-Agent Framework for structured CBT dialogue generation
items.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in mental health support, existing approaches often provide unstructured emotional responses and struggle to deliver structured, evidence-based interventions such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Existing CBT dialogue datasets also lack sufficient clinical depth and phase-specific patient resistance. To address these limitations, we construct the CCD-CBT Dataset, a multi-phase CBT dialogue corpus integrating expert textbook knowledge with real-world doctor–patient interactions sourced from Haodf Online and other medical consultation websites. The dataset contains 1314 samples covering the four standard CBT treatment phases, from initial assessment to termination, with an average dialogue length of 132.12 turns. The average utterance length is 61.34 Chinese characters for patients and 97.05 Chinese characters for therapists. Based on this dataset, we propose CCD-MAF, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework guided by the Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram (CCD). CCD-MAF decomposes the CBT counseling process into macro-phase planning, meso-state tracking, and micro-technique execution, enabling dynamic modeling of patients’ cognitive structures and targeted interventions. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B as the therapist component within CCD-MAF and conduct single-turn and multi-turn clinical simulations. The evaluation distinguishes system-level comparisons among independently operated systems from therapist-component substitution comparisons within the shared CCD-MAF framework. Results indicate that CCD-MAF demonstrates strong performance in Cognitive Therapy Scale (CTS)-based simulated evaluations. In the component-substitution setting, the fine-tuned therapist component achieves the best performance among the evaluated therapist components under the same CCD-MAF framework. Ablation studies further support the contribution of the proposed multi-agent mechanism. This study provides an interpretable and clinically structured framework for developing AI psychological assistants, with its effectiveness evaluated in simulated counseling settings.

items.title: Center for Anticipation 2.0: Human, Artificial Intelligence, and Domain Expert in the Study of Possible Futures
items.abstract: Center for Anticipation 2.0 is an independent research initiative founded by Sergey Antonovich Kravchenko, continuing the work of the original Center for Anticipation (2008–2018). The project investigates how possible futures are represented in human experience through dreams, intuition, premonitions, altered states of consciousness, and anticipatory processes. Particular attention is given to the transition from an initial subjective experience to interpretation, prospective formulation, independent verification, preparedness, and responsible action. The research framework combines phenomenological documentation, the Method of Significant Associations, temporal analysis, alternative explanatory models, and collaboration among human researchers, artificial intelligence, and domain experts. The project distinguishes ordinary psychological anticipation and unconscious inference from the more demanding hypothesis of precognition. The existence of an unusual subjective experience is not treated as evidence of information transfer from the future. All prospective claims require time-stamped documentation, clearly defined verification criteria, consideration of unsuccessful predictions, and independent assessment. The Center aims to develop transparent research protocols, a cumulative archive of documented observations, and opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration. This publication presents the conceptual and methodological foundations of Center for Anticipation 2.0 (Version 1.0, October 2026). The Russian and English texts are provided as two language versions of the same publication. Researchers in psychology, consciousness studies, philosophy of time, cognitive science, statistics, and artificial intelligence are invited to contribute critical discussion, methodological proposals, and collaborative research.

items.title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a principal recipe for improving the reasoning of large language models (LLMs). It rests on the assumption that the checker scoring each response is itself correct. In practice, rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. This work surveys 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors. We ask what errors verifiers make, how they affect training, which mitigations work against which errors, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric- and judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. The evidence suggests that the structure of an error matters more than its rate. Random errors mostly slow learning, though under a fixed budget or KL regularization they also lower final accuracy. False positives that the policy can learn to trigger can cause plateaus or collapse, sometimes even with a low initial error rate. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or accepts depends on what it checks and who built it, not on its family. Its errors shift as the policy improves, and most mitigations have been tested against only one kind of error. We compile the findings into comparison tables, reconcile apparent conflicts in the literature, and propose a reporting protocol to make future results comparable.

items.title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
items.abstract: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.

items.title: Clinical Effectiveness, Safety, and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Insulin Management Systems in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into insulin management through decision-support systems, adaptive bolus calculators, conversational platforms, and automated insulin delivery (AID) technologies. However, the clinical effectiveness and safety of AI-assisted insulin management remain uncertain. Objective: To systematically evaluate evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating AI-assisted insulin management systems in individuals with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for RCTs evaluating AI-enabled insulin management interventions in insulin-treated individuals with diabetes. Eligible studies compared AI-based systems with standard care, clinician-guided insulin titration, conventional bolus calculators, or other AID algorithms. Outcomes included glycemic control, insulin titration, safety, and implementation-related measures. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Results: We included seven RCTs published between 2020 and 2025. Interventions comprised clinical decision-support systems, adaptive bolus calculators, conversational AI platforms, neural-network-based artificial pancreas algorithms, and exercise-aware AID systems. AI-assisted interventions consistently demonstrated favorable safety profiles, with no increase in severe hypoglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or serious adverse events. Some systems, particularly fully automated closed-loop platforms and conversational AI-guided insulin titration, showed improvements in time in range, glucose control, adherence, and insulin optimization. User acceptance and adherence emerged as important determinants of effectiveness. Conclusions: Current randomized evidence suggests that AI-assisted insulin management systems are safe, feasible, and capable of achieving glycemic outcomes comparable to conventional care. Although certain technologies demonstrate promising clinical benefits, the evidence base remains limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up durations, and heterogeneity across interventions. Larger, long-term randomized trials are needed to establish comparative effectiveness, optimize human–AI interaction, and support broader clinical implementation.

items.title: Co-producing sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries on the MOSE megaproject: Media frames of continuity, stability and transformation in Venice
items.abstract: In Europe, sea level rise adaptation is strongly reliant on technological and engineering solutions. Megaprojects such as Venice’s mobile floodgate system MOSE are meant to provide protection to coastal areas. Due to their complexity and sizeable impact, however, megaprojects tend to be highly contentious. This article explores the interplay of sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries in MOSE and how they build a collective past, present, and imagined future. Using data from Italian media, we identify frames that combine sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries that co-produce a legitimation of MOSE through techno-optimistic ideas of uniqueness and innovation, thereby illustrating how cultural and historical values shape spatial and sociotechnical imaginaries to construct the acceptance of wide-scale megaprojects. However, imaginaries of megaprojects also reveal contradictions: when ecological issues are framed as invasive events, imaginaries reject techno-optimism and place nature at the top of the hierarchy of space and place. Our study helps to deepen the conceptual understanding of sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries by looking at how they intertwine with temporal and spatial-hierarchical dimensions.

items.title: CoCA: Criterion-Aware Credit Assignment for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) evaluates responses against explicit criteria to construct rewards, offering a viable way to train large language models on open-ended tasks. However, standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards and assign uniform token advantages, leaving structured rubric supervision underutilized. Recent work seeks finer-grained guidance by treating rubrics as privileged information to derive self-distillation targets, but the resulting learning signal is not grounded in criterion outcomes and can lead to reward degradation. This motivates us to reframe the problem as criterion-aware credit assignment, where privileged rubric information serves as a relevance cue for credit allocation rather than a source of imitation targets. Accordingly, we propose CoCA, which derives criterion-level credits from group-relative outcomes and allocates them across tokens based on criterion-induced distribution shifts, yielding both outcome-grounded and fine-grained learning signals. Empirically, CoCA achieves an average gain of +4.2% over standard rubric-based RL across medicine and science benchmarks, demonstrating more effective learning on open-ended tasks.

items.title: Cognitive workload across subjective and electrodermal measures in relation to previous-night sleep
items.abstract: Introduction Cognitive workload is commonly assessed using both subjective and physiological indicators, although these measures may reflect different aspects of task-related strain. Sleep duration may further modify perceived task demand without producing proportional changes in physiological activation. This study examined the association between perceived cognitive workload and electrodermal task reactivity, and explored whether previous-night short sleep was associated with higher subjective workload without increased electrodermal activation. Methods A total of 52 adults were initially assessed; two were excluded due to violation of predefined eligibility criteria, resulting in a final analytical sample of 50 participants. Participants reported previous-night sleep duration and subjective sleep quality, completed a 5-min resting baseline, and then performed the Determination Test from the Vienna Test System. Electrodermal activity was recorded continuously during baseline and task performance, while perceived workload was assessed after the task using the NASA Task Load Index. Task-related electrodermal reactivity was calculated as GSR task–baseline difference, and participants were classified into short-sleep (< 7 h) and normal-sleep (≥7 h) groups. Results NASA-TLX total workload was not significantly associated with GSR task–baseline difference (rho = 0.126, p = 0.383). In the uncorrected threshold-based comparison, participants with short sleep reported higher perceived workload than those with normal sleep (64.44 ± 8.31 vs. 58.70 ± 9.57; p = 0.027), whereas GSR task–baseline difference was nearly identical between groups (4.57 ± 2.19 vs. 4.61 ± 2.93 μS; p = 0.884). However, the workload difference did not survive FDR correction across exploratory subgroup comparisons and should therefore be interpreted as a nominal finding. Discussion Overall, perceived workload and electrodermal reactivity showed limited correspondence, whereas the sleep-related analyses did not provide consistent evidence of an association with either outcome.

items.title: Col-Ovo: Smartphone-based artificial intelligence for rapid counting of Aedes mosquito eggs under field conditions
items.abstract: Abstract Background The global expansion of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes has intensified the transmission of dengue, Zika, and chikungunya viruses, increasing the need for scalable surveillance tools. OviCol, a low-cost ovitrap-based strategy integrating mosquito monitoring and control, has shown promise for community-based vector management. However, large-scale deployment generates thousands of oviposition substrates that require labor-intensive manual egg counting, creating a major operational bottleneck. This study aimed to develop and evaluate Col-Ovo, an artificial intelligence-based system for automated counting of Ae. aegypti eggs from smartphone images collected under routine field conditions. Methods Col-Ovo was developed using a YOLOv11m object-detection model trained on 275 oviposition substrates (20.5 cm strips) collected through operational surveillance activities. Images were captured in situ using smartphones without preprocessing and included samples stained with bioattractants (blackstrap molasses and Saccharomyces cerevisiae ) as well as sand and particulate debris. The system was designed to tolerate image compression generated by messaging platforms, such as WhatsApp. Performance was assessed by comparing automated egg counts with expert manual counts and virtual-human counts conducted through the OviLab platform using >200% image magnification. Agreement between methods was evaluated using correlation and concordance analyses. Results Col-Ovo successfully detected and quantified Ae. aegypti eggs under challenging field conditions, including heavily stained and debris-contaminated substrates. Col-Ovo showed strong agreement with human evaluators (Spearman ρ = 0.91; Lin’s ρc = 0.89; MAE = 22.1 eggs) and with OviLab counts, with no significant difference in paired comparisons ( P = 0.252). The system reduced processing time from approximately 15 min per substrate to less than 3 s, representing a substantial increase in operational efficiency. Performance remained robust when analyzing compressed smartphone images shared through common messaging applications. Conclusions Col-Ovo provides a rapid, accurate, and scalable approach for quantifying Ae. aegypti eggs from smartphone images. By eliminating the need for specialized equipment or image preprocessing, the system addresses a critical barrier to large-scale ovitrap surveillance. Integrated with the OviLab platform, Col-Ovo offers a flexible digital infrastructure that can strengthen vector surveillance, support timely public health responses, and facilitate the expansion of community-based mosquito control programs.

items.title: Collapse, Repair, and Drift: Dissecting Fine Tuning Dynamics in Speech Language Models
items.abstract: Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is commonly monitored through training and evaluation loss, but loss does not fully characterize how model functionality evolves along the same trajectory. We study this gap through dialect adaptation of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$. Character error rate (CER) reveals pronounced transient collapse and recovery whose severity and temporal structure are only weakly reflected by loss. Bidirectional layer patching reveals strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize during recovery. Pairwise gradient similarity alone does not reliably indicate optimization stability, whereas raw gradient spectral analysis provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization: successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, while failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent fluctuations. Finally, AdamW update transfer bypasses pronounced early collapse, yet substantial Mandarin degradation still emerges later in training. These results motivate three separable SFT dynamics: collapse, repair, and drift, and show that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation.

items.title: Communicating Uncertainty in AI-Supported Nurse Scheduling: Expert Co-Design and Evaluation of an Explainable AI Prototype
items.abstract: Nurse scheduling is a complex optimization problem in which nurses are assigned to shifts to meet staffing demands while complying with working-time limits, qualification requirements, and other operational and regulatory constraints. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to support this process by forecasting future staffing needs and providing advice on how to improve shift scheduling. Effective human-AI collaboration in nurse scheduling requires users to understand, interpret, and appropriately act on AI forecasts and advice. However, it remains insufficiently understood how healthcare professionals use transparency mechanisms like uncertainty communication and AI advice explanations when making staffing decisions. Applying a human-centered design approach, we iteratively developed a prototype decision support system for nurse scheduling and evaluated it through a mixed-methods user study with expert users. Using thematic analysis, questionnaire data, and eye tracking, we examine how healthcare professionals interact with the system and how uncertainty communication and explanations of AI advice influence understanding, decision confidence, trust, and usability. We found that the uncertainty communicated in AI forecasts was frequently misinterpreted and reduced decision confidence. Explanations were generally perceived positively, but did not significantly affect decision confidence or advice acceptance. We conclude with eight design implications derived from our findings, providing insights for the design of more transparent and effective AI-supported decision support tools in healthcare.

items.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
items.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.

items.title: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED APPROACHES TO FORECASTING AND OPTIMIZATION OF COMPLEX SYSTEMS
items.abstract: Forecasting and optimization form an integrated foundation for the intelligent management of complex systems in industry, logistics, energy, transportation, and service operations. The interaction of multiple components, changing operating conditions, and interconnected decisions creates valuable opportunities for data-driven modeling and adaptive resource allocation. This study presents a comparative literature-based analysis of statistical forecasting, machine learning, deep learning, mathematical optimization, and reinforcement learning approaches. Their suitability is examined in relation to temporal patterns, explanatory variables, uncertainty representation, computational requirements, and decision objectives. Particular attention is given to hybrid architectures that connect probabilistic forecasts with optimization models and continuously updated decisions. The synthesis establishes a conceptual framework for evaluating forecasting quality alongside operational performance and identifies promising directions for intelligent management of dynamic complex systems.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness of conventional nursing versus data-driven predictive nursing models in orthopedic trauma patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Orthopedic injuries have necessitated the adoption of appropriate nursing interventions to promote favorable healing and minimize risks and complications associated with these conditions. In recent times, predictive nursing models that use artificial intelligence have generated considerable interest, particularly for comparison with traditional nursing interventions. To determine the comparative effectiveness of traditional nursing interventions versus data-driven predictive nursing models in orthopedic injury cases. A systematic review of 33 studies, including randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, quasi-experiments, and machine-learning-based prediction studies, was conducted. Pooled odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were computed by employing a random-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis approach. Heterogeneity between studies was measured with I-squared statistics, while publication bias was detected with Egger’s test and funnel plot analyses. There was a statistically significant improvement in all intervention categories compared to the control group. Traditional and perioperative nursing interventions had an overall OR of 2.13 (95% CI 1.74–2.61), whereas postoperative rehabilitation interventions had an OR of 1.97 (95% CI 1.37–2.84). The machine learning-based predictive models had an OR of 2.26 (1.89–2.71), whereas the predictive nursing decision-support systems had an OR of 2.14 (1.70–2.68). Prognostic studies also had OR 2.27 (1.82–2.83). The heterogeneity was at most moderate, and there was no publication bias except in prognostic studies. Predictive and conventional nursing strategies both significantly improve orthopedic trauma outcomes, with predictive models offering greater potential for individualized care.

items.title: Complementary Error Profiles of Human Readers and Large Language Models in Detecting AI-Generated Chest Radiographs: A Comparative Reader Study
items.abstract: Abstract Frontier large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models can generate realistic chest radiographs, raising concerns for dataset integrity when provenance metadata are absent. We compared authenticity judgments by two radiologists, two nonradiologist physicians, and three frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8) on 160 posteroanterior radiographs: 40 real NIH ChestX-ray14 images and 120 synthetic images generated from text by three pipelines. Each evaluator judged every image once; the LLM evaluation was repeated twice 3 months later. Balanced accuracy was the primary metric, given 75% synthetic prevalence. The two best evaluators reached nearly identical balanced accuracy from opposite operating points: Gemini 3.5 Flash had the highest point estimate (77.9%; specificity 100%, sensitivity 55.8%) and RAD1 was a close second (75.8%; specificity 55.0%, sensitivity 96.7%), a paired difference of − 2.1 percentage points (95% CI, − 5.8 to 1.2). On repetition, LLM judgments were not fully reproducible and this ordering did not hold. Nonradiologists performed near chance. All four human readers detected diffusion-generated images at 82–100%, whereas the radiologists misclassified 38–45% of real images and the conservative LLMs reached perfect specificity yet detected only 32–72% of LLM-generated images. With laterality markers and borders masked, specificity was 62.5% (Gemini) and 85.0% (GPT-5.5) against 90–100% in same-day unmasked runs. Interevaluator agreement was low throughout (Fleiss’ kappa among LLMs 0.213). A frequency-domain baseline reached 98.3% balanced accuracy within this dataset but 12% sensitivity on a held-out generator. Human readers and LLMs failed on different images; visual authenticity assessment alone may be insufficient for provenance verification.

items.title: Computational approaches to deep learning–driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review
items.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

items.title: Construction and content validation of an OBE-AI-CED integrated teaching framework for the liquor factory design course in local undergraduate universities: a modified Delphi study
items.abstract: The digital, intelligent and green transformation of the Chinese baijiu industry has introduced new competency demands for liquor engineering education. The Liquor Factory Design course is a comprehensive upper-level engineering design course for students in the liquor engineering program that combines knowledge of brewing technology, chemical engineering, engineering drawing, brewing equipment, energy-saving and environmental protection, and production management. However, the course in local undergraduate universities still has several problems, such as an unclear design task chain, a lack of authentic engineering contexts, ambiguous boundaries for the use of artificial intelligence, and an assessment approach that focuses too much on the final product rather than the learning process. The above problems may limit the all-round development of students’ engineering design abilities. Given the above problems, this paper builds an OBE-AI-CED integrated teaching system for the Liquor Factory Design course by integrating Outcome-Based Education, Artificial Intelligence and Complex Engineering Design. A modified Delphi method was employed to examine the content validity and refine the framework. Two rounds of expert consultations were conducted with university teachers, engineering technicians from Baijiu Enterprise, and experts from an engineering design institution. The first round of results showed that, although most experts agreed that a framework was needed, they raised concerns about the limits of AI application, the viability of sustained cooperation between enterprises and mentors, a lack of genuine engineering resources, and an unfinished chain of evaluation evidence. Based on expert feedback, AI was repositioned as a tool for learning support and design reasoning rather than automatic design generation. A complex engineering design task chain was established, including production scale determination, process flow design, material balance, equipment selection, workshop layout, energy conservation and environmental protection, drawing expression, and design defense. In addition, industrial case libraries, equipment parameter databases, engineering drawing resources, and an evidence-based assessment mechanism were incorporated into the framework. The second-round results showed increased mean scores, reduced coefficients of variation, and greater concordance among participating experts. These results reflect expert consensus on the revised framework, while student learning effectiveness was not evaluated in this study. The proposed framework may support the transformation of the Liquor Factory Design course from a report-oriented model to a competence-oriented model and provide a reference for cultivating complex engineering design competence in liquor engineering programs in local undergraduate universities in China.

items.title: Consumer Behavioural Insights for AI-Enabled Personalized Food Waste Reduction in Restaurants
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly enabling restaurants to deliver personalized customer experiences while supporting sustainable business practices. However, the effectiveness of AI-enabled interventions depends on understanding the behavioural factors that influence consumer food waste. This study examines consumer behaviour related to restaurant food waste and explores how behavioural insights can inform AI-driven personalization strategies for food waste reduction. The research is grounded in the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) and is based on primary data collected from 100 restaurant consumers in the Mumbai Suburban region using a structured questionnaire. The study assessed six behavioural constructs: awareness, attitude, behavioural factors, psychological factors, social factors, and willingness to act towards food waste reduction. Descriptive analysis revealed that respondents demonstrated relatively high levels of awareness (Mean = 3.89) and positive attitudes (Mean = 3.92) towards reducing food waste. Psychological factors (Mean = 3.81) and social factors (Mean = 3.64) also indicated favourable behavioural orientations. However, behavioural practices recorded comparatively lower scores (Mean = 3.45), suggesting an attitude–behaviour gap in responsible food consumption. Respondents also expressed a positive willingness to adopt food waste reduction practices (Mean = 3.76), indicating the potential for targeted behavioural interventions. Based on these findings, the study proposes an AI-driven consumer insight framework that can support restaurants in designing personalized food waste reduction strategies, including portion-size recommendations, smart menu suggestions, and digital nudges. Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for managerial decision-making, the framework demonstrates how consumer behavioural data can be leveraged to enhance AI-enabled customer engagement and sustainability initiatives. The study contributes to the growing discourse on AI in Business and Marketing by illustrating the role of behavioural insights in developing customer-centric and sustainable restaurant practices. The findings offer practical implications for restaurant managers seeking to integrate AI-enabled personalization with food waste reduction initiatives in the HORECA sector. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Consumer Behaviour, Food Waste, Restaurant Management, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Sustainability, HORECA.

items.title: Consumer Decision-Making in Digital Commerce: Effects of Virtual Influencer Motive Attributions on Trust, Perceived Risk, and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In AI-enabled digital commerce, consumers evaluate virtual influencers (VIs) not only through source characteristics but also by inferring why they create content and recommend products. This study examines how perceived intrinsic and commercially oriented extrinsic motives are associated with trust, perceived risk, and purchase intention. Survey data from 295 South Korean consumers aged 20–39 were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 23.0 for descriptive and reliability analyses and IBM SPSS Amos 24.0 for confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Perceived intrinsic motivation was positively associated with trust but was not significantly associated with perceived risk or directly with purchase intention. Perceived extrinsic motivation was negatively associated with trust and purchase intention and positively associated with perceived risk. Trust was positively associated with purchase intention, whereas the conditional association of perceived risk was nonsignificant. Supplementary bootstrap analyses supported specific indirect associations through trust for both motive attributions, consistent with full (indirect-only) mediation for intrinsic motivation and partial mediation for extrinsic motivation within the specified model. Neither specific indirect association through perceived risk was significant. These findings distinguish consumers’ confidence in a recommending persona from their uncertainty about a recommended purchase and identify trust as a central statistical mediator of motive attribution and purchase intention in VI marketing.

items.title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

items.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
items.abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

items.title: Cough Sounds for the Recognition of Multiclass Respiratory Diseases With Artificial Intelligence: A Review
items.abstract: Respiratory diseases such as asthma, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), tuberculosis, and COVID-19 require timely recognition and appropriate medical evaluation. Cough is a common symptom of many respiratory conditions and contains acoustic characteristics that can provide useful information for disease recognition. This report presents a review of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for recognizing multiclass respiratory diseases using cough sounds. The review examines cough datasets, audio preprocessing, feature extraction, and Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques used for cough analysis. Common methods include noise reduction, cough segmentation, Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), Mel-spectrograms, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The review also discusses applications, advantages, limitations, and evaluation methods. Findings indicate that AI-based cough analysis has potential as a non-invasive and accessible supportive screening technology. However, challenges such as limited datasets, background noise, class imbalance, recording-device variations, similar acoustic patterns, model generalization, privacy, and clinical validation remain. Future research should focus on larger and diverse datasets, explainable AI, smartphone-based systems, multimodal analysis, and clinical validation for reliable respiratory disease recognition.

items.title: Creating Digital Public Value in Platform States
items.abstract: As states adopt platform-based models of public governance, understanding how institutional capabilities and governance arrangements translate into societal value has become a central concern for public administration research. No quantitative model had jointly tested how public digital capability, data governance, and platform governance interact to shape digital platform use and digital public value creation in emerging economies such as Morocco. This chapter develops and empirically validates an integrative tripartite structural model grounded in Public Value Theory, New Public Management, and Sociotechnical Theory, using PLS-SEM on a sample of 350 Moroccan public employees, civil servants, and citizens. All seven hypotheses were confirmed at p < 0.001: public digital capability and platform governance emerged as the strongest direct determinants of platform use, which fully mediates digital public value creation. The chapter offers theoretical and managerial insights for decision-makers engaged in digital transformation in emerging platform states.

items.abstract: The global emergence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacilli represents one of the major global public health challenges today, requiring structured interventions for antimicrobial stewardship. The guidelines of the Brazilian Society of Infectious Diseases (SBI) establish rigorous, evidence-based therapeutic protocols for the treatment of severe infections caused by carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii. The SBI emphasizes the selection of initial empirical coverage grounded in local epidemiology and microbiological profiles, the optimization of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters, as well as mandatory reassessment at 48 to 72 hours to promote early therapeutic de-escalation. This article presents an expanded narrative and critical-analytical review on the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a clinical decision support tool to enable and operationalize the implementation of SBI guidelines at the hospital bedside. The study delves into the main applications of AI, including individualized prediction of resistance risk upon admission, accelerated predictive antibiograms via mass spectrometry and deep learning, real-time precision dosing, and natural language processing for auditing narrative records in electronic health records, critically contrasting them with the reasons justifying the absence of AI in official protocols of other international medical organizations and the SBI itself. From the perspective of Brazilian regulation, the study analyzes in detail compliance with the General Data Protection Law (LGPD) and Resolution CFM No. 2,454/2026 of the Federal Council of Medicine, which categorically prohibits prescriptive autonomy for automated systems, ensuring the centrality of medical judgment and enshrining the 'human-in-the-loop' paradigm.

items.title: Cybercrime in India under the New Criminal Laws: Emerging Challenges in Investigation, Digital Evidence and Criminal Justice
items.abstract: The rapid growth of digital technology has changed the way people communicate, conduct business, access financial services and interact with government institutions. At the same time, this transformation has created new opportunities for criminal activity. Cybercrime today includes online financial fraud, identity theft, unauthorised access to computer systems, cyberstalking, impersonation, data theft, social media offences and technologically facilitated forms of traditional crime. The investigation and prosecution of such offences present difficulties that differ from those associated with conventional crimes because electronic evidence can be easily altered, deleted, transferred and stored across multiple jurisdictions. The introduction of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 represents a significant transformation of India's criminal justice framework. This paper examines the implications of the new criminal laws for cybercrime investigation, digital evidence and criminal justice administration. It also considers the continuing importance of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the constitutional protection of privacy and due process. The paper adopts a doctrinal and analytical methodology based on legislation, judicial decisions and authoritative legal materials. It argues that legislative reform by itself cannot adequately address the complexity of cybercrime. Effective enforcement requires trained investigators, modern forensic infrastructure, rapid preservation of electronic evidence, coordination between investigative agencies and service providers, and appropriate safeguards for individual rights. The paper further examines emerging challenges associated with artificial intelligence, deepfakes, digital impersonation and sophisticated online fraud. It concludes that India's new criminal laws provide an important foundation for dealing with cybercrime, but their success will ultimately depend upon effective implementation, technological capacity and a careful balance between criminal enforcement and constitutional liberties.

items.title: Data Analytics and AI
items.abstract: Data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming geotechnical monitoring by extracting insights from large sensor datasets. This chapter covers analytics objectives (trend detection, anomaly identification, and prediction) and data types (time-series, spatial, imagery, and point clouds). We discuss preprocessing: cleaning, labeling, and metadata standards. Exploratory analysis and visualization techniques are highlighted. Statistical methods (trend tests, change-point detection) and uncertainty quantification are reviewed. Time-series tools include filtering, smoothing, ARIMA, and Kalman filters (with equations). We survey anomaly detection approaches: simple thresholds, statistical tests, and unsupervised ML (clustering, PCA/autoencoders). Supervised learning for classification/regression (feature selection, model validation, and metrics like ROC/AUC) is covered. Deep learning methods (LSTMs/RNNs for sequences, CNNs/Transformers for images, PointNets for clouds) and physics-informed neural networks are introduced. Digital twins and the integration of ML with geomechanical models are discussed. Real-time analytics, streaming, and edge inference (MLOps) are addressed, as are alarm logic, false-positive management, and human-in-the-loop frameworks. We emphasize explainability, model validation, and regulatory guidance. Two worked examples illustrate a Kalman filter update and an ROC curve calculation. Tables compare algorithms (data needs, latency, interpretability), and a mermaid diagram shows an analytics pipeline. items.title: Data Analytics and Big Data in Cybersecurity Threat Detection: A Critical Review of Techniques, Challenges, and Emerging Directions
items.abstract: The increasing sophistication and scale of cyber threats have intensified the need for analytical methods capable of processing high-volume, high-velocity, and heterogeneous security data. This critical review synthesizes 38 scholarly sources identified through a structured Google Scholar search and a PRISMA-informed screening workflow to examine the role of data analytics and big data in cybersecurity threat detection. The review considers signature-based, anomaly-based, behaviour-based, machine-learning, and deep-learning approaches, together with operational challenges and emerging directions. Across heterogeneous datasets and application settings, machine-learning and deep-learning methods offer strong representation-learning and pattern-recognition capabilities, while anomaly- and behaviour-based approaches remain important for identifying previously unseen or context-dependent activity. Their practical effectiveness, however, depends on data quality, labelling, class balance, computational resources, interpretability, privacy, and the operating environment. Because the underlying studies use different datasets, tasks, metrics, and validation designs, the evidence does not support a universal ranking of detection approaches. Current research increasingly emphasises explainable artificial intelligence, federated learning, privacy-preserving analytics, hybrid detection architectures, and real-time processing. The review concludes that robust cybersecurity analytics requires context-appropriate combinations of complementary techniques rather than reliance on a single universally superior model.

items.title: Decomposing and Predicting Annotation Disagreement in Harmful Content Across Languages
items.abstract: Annotator disagreement is increasingly recognized as a meaningful property of subjective tasks, rather than merely noise to be removed. Predicting which items are likely to be contested could help allocate annotation effort and route difficult cases to human review. We propose predicting disagreement from interpretable semantic properties of the text. An LLM answers a set of binary questions covering harmful-content characteristics, disagreement-related cues such as borderline severity and missing context, and language-sensitive cues such as local slurs. A classifier predicts disagreement from these answers, and we analyze which questions contribute most to the predictions. Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, our structured question features outperform direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the strongest text-based baselines by 5.0 points. A compact subset of eight questions performs within 1.5 ROC-AUC points of the full twenty-question set. In leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, models retain roughly 90-95% of their in-domain ROC-AUC. Across models and datasets, questions about derogation, missing context, and decision boundaries serve as the strongest predictors, suggesting that what makes harmful content contested is partly observable in the text.

items.title: Deconstructing the Menstrual Barrier to Education: Examining Psychological, Social, and Structural Barriers in the Somali Region of Ethiopia
items.abstract: Documentation detailing the relative inaccessibility of education in Ethiopia’s Somali Region continues to grow. Structural barriers—including limited access to school programs, a shortage of qualified teachers, insufficient funding, and scarce learning resources—act as compounding disadvantages for all learners. These realities are further exacerbated for adolescent girls by inadequate access to dedicated gender-responsive washrooms (private latrines and clean water) essential for Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM). When girls lack access to private, gender responsive facilities, physical limitations become a catalyst for acute psychological distress. This psychological distress (marked by shame and embarrassment), combined with social pressures (leading to planned absenteeism) and diminished cognitive engagement (distraction caused by the ongoing anxiety of leakage), results in lower overall attendance and academic achievement. These factors define the parameters of social disapproval surrounding female education. The social disapproval associated with menstruation directly impacts girls' intentions to attend school while menstruating, acting as a socially constructed mechanism of exclusion that violates the fundamental right to education enshrined by UNESCO. This study (n=450) compares girls with access to re-useable MHM kits, paired with health education to a control group. This represents a baseline study to then revisit longitudinally to see if having access to reliable MHM changes beliefs and behaviours around school attendance and engagement during menstruation. A theory-driven principal component analysis explored key factors influencing school attendance and engagement for girls in the Somali Region of Ethiopia.

items.title: Deepfakes and bots in digital disinformation driven by malicious artificial intelligence
items.abstract: In an increasingly uncertain digital environment, how do we know if what we see is real? Deepfakes, which include videos with fake faces, synthetic audio, and manipulated documents, along with social bots that interact and persuade as if they were humans, represent a growing threat driven by malicious artificial intelligence. These technologies not only spread disinformation but also generate collective emotions such as fear, indignation, and distrust, affecting democratic stability and social cohesion. Faced with this reality, this article develops a bibliometric study and a scoping review of the literature (2014-2024) based on 316 documents indexed in Scopus, with the purpose of identifying trends, influential authors, methodological approaches, and research gaps on the use of artificial intelligence in disinformation. The results show an annual growth of 97%, an average age of 2.2 years per document, 19.7 average citations, and an h-index of 37, evidencing the sustained expansion and scientific interest in the detection of deepfakes and bots as central challenges of the digital ecosystem. Production is concentrated in India, the United States, and China. The co-occurrence analysis confirms the main research axes in deepfake detection, deep learning, and CNNs, along with the growing prominence of synthetic speech, diffusion models, and the economic and social effects of social media. Future research should address the role of AI in political communication, in particular its links to disinformation, polarization, and emotional influence, as well as the impact of the EU AI Act, the need for standardised metrics, and the emergence of transnational frameworks for digital governance.

items.title: Deliberation Within AI: A Reproducible Pipeline for Multi-Agent Deliberation Simulation
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have renewed interest in whether large language models can simulate aspects of public deliberation. Current deliberation simulations remain methodologically fragile: fluent conversational outputs are often treated as evidence of deliberative quality despite limited reproducibility, weak safeguards for viewpoint diversity, and limited systematic evaluation. This article argues that AI-deliberation simulations can function as credible analytical instruments only if they incorporate infrastructures for reproducibility, plurality preservation, and deliberative quality assessment. The article develops a stage-structured method for deliberative simulation combining persona validation, plurality auditing, and discourse-quality assessment within a reproducible pipeline. The framework is presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and evaluated through a simulation study on the June 2023 Swiss federal referendum on the Climate and Innovation Act together with a batch replication study comparing direct and structured deliberation architectures. The findings show that, as an integrated theory-driven architecture, the structured pipeline generates more stable deliberative dynamics than unconstrained interaction, including clearer plurality preservation and more coherent opinion updating. At the same time, the simulations remain below human minipublics in terms of contextual grounding and justificatory depth. The article positions AI-deliberation simulations as methodological infrastructures for cumulative and empirically testable research on AI-supported deliberation in digital governance.
